sumber: KSSM Form 2 Mathematics DSKP (KPM), English for the Dual Language Programme. Written for the app.

t: Arithmetic sequence: add a common difference.

nota.t: A pattern is an arrangement of numbers, objects or shapes that follows a rule. Number patterns are found from the difference or ratio between terms. Special patterns include even and odd numbers, square numbers, Pascal's triangle and the Fibonacci numbers.
A sequence is a set of numbers arranged by a pattern. T₁ is the first term and Tₙ the nth term. Missing terms are found by continuing the pattern.
A pattern can be written in words, numbers or algebra. For a sequence with common difference d, the nth term is Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
Example: 4, 9, 14, … a = 4, d = 5, so Tₙ = 5n − 1 and T₂₀ = 99.

t: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd

nota.t: Expansion multiplies every term outside the brackets by every term inside, then collects like terms. Special cases: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².

v.c: Expansion as the area of a rectangle

nota.t: Factorisation is the reverse of expansion: common factors, difference of two squares, quadratic trinomials and grouping four terms.
Algebraic fractions are added or subtracted with a common denominator, multiplied straight across, and divided by multiplying by the reciprocal. Factorise first to cancel common factors.

t: Subject of a formula: the variable on its own on the left.
Substitute values to find a variable.

nota.t: An algebraic formula links variables, such as A = πr² or v = u + at. Values are found by substituting known values into the formula.
3.2 Subject of a Formula and Substitution
The subject of a formula is the variable written alone on one side. Change the subject by doing inverse operations on both sides, then substitute values.

v.c: Changing the subject of a formula

nota.t: A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles. A regular n-sided polygon has n lines of symmetry. A regular hexagon can be constructed by marking six points round a circle using the radius.
4.2 Interior and Exterior Angles of Polygons
Sum of interior angles = (n − 2) × 180°. Each interior angle of a regular polygon = (n − 2) × 180° ÷ n. Exterior angles always add up to 360°, so each exterior angle = 360° ÷ n.
Example: exterior angle 30° → number of sides = 360° ÷ 30° = 12.

v.c: Interior angles of a regular pentagon

nota.t: A circle is the set of points the same distance from the centre. Parts: radius, diameter, circumference, chord, arc, sector and segment. The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre.
5.3 Circumference and Area of a Circle
Circumference = 2πr = πd. Area = πr². Use π = 3.142 or 22/7.
Arc length = (θ/360°) × 2πr and sector area = (θ/360°) × πr², where θ is the angle at the centre.
Example: r = 7 cm, θ = 90°. Arc = 11 cm; sector area = 38.5 cm².
3D shapes have length, width and height. Prisms and cylinders have two equal parallel bases; pyramids and cones meet at an apex; a sphere has no edges or vertices. Euler: F + V − E = 2 for polyhedra.
A net is a 2D shape that folds into a 3D shape. A cube's net has six squares; a cylinder's net has two circles and a rectangle whose length equals the circumference.

Surface area is the total area of all faces: cylinder 2πr² + 2πrh, cone πr² + πrl, sphere 4πr². Volume: prism and cylinder = base area × height; pyramid and cone = ⅓ × base area × height; sphere = ⁴⁄₃πr³.
Example: cone r = 3 cm, h = 7 cm. V = ⅓ × 22/7 × 9 × 7 = 66 cm³.

v.c: Surface area and volume of a cone

nota.t: The Cartesian plane has an x-axis and y-axis crossing at the origin (0, 0), dividing it into four quadrants. A point is written (x, y).
Distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²], from Pythagoras' theorem.
The midpoint of a line segment = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2), the average of the coordinates.
A function gives each input exactly one output, written f(x). One-to-one and many-to-one relations are functions; one-to-many is not.
Draw a graph by making a table of values, choosing a scale, plotting points and joining them with a straight line or smooth curve. Read values from the graph.
Speed = distance ÷ time, in km/h or m/s. Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
Example: 150 km in 2.5 h → 60 km/h. 72 km/h = 20 m/s.
Acceleration = (final speed − initial speed) ÷ time, in m/s². Negative acceleration is deceleration.
Example: 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s → 4 m/s².

t: y = mx + c: m is the gradient, c the y-intercept.

nota.t: Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), vertical change ÷ horizontal change. Lines rising to the right have positive gradient, falling lines negative; horizontal lines zero; vertical lines undefined.

t: Translation (a, b): (x, y) → (x + a, y + b).

nota.t: A transformation changes an object's position, orientation or size. Isometries (translation, reflection, rotation) keep shape and size, so object and image are congruent.

A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction, written as a column vector (a, b). A reflection flips an object in a mirror line: in the x-axis (x, y) → (x, −y), in the y-axis (x, y) → (−x, y).

A rotation turns an object about a centre by an angle, clockwise or anticlockwise. 90° anticlockwise about the origin: (x, y) → (−y, x). Translation, reflection and rotation are isometries; a shape has rotational symmetry of order n if it looks the same n times in a full turn.

t: Median: the middle of ordered data.

nota.t: Measures of central tendency: mean (sum ÷ number of values; Σfx ÷ Σf for a frequency table), median (middle value after ordering) and mode (most frequent value). The median suits data with extreme values.
Example: x = 2, 3, 4, 5 with f = 3, 5, 8, 4. Mean = 73/20 = 3.65; mode = 4; median = 4.

t: P(A) = outcomes in A ÷ size of the sample space.

nota.t: Experimental probability = number of times an event happens ÷ number of trials. As trials increase, it approaches the theoretical probability.
Example: a 6 appears 12 times in 60 rolls → P = 1/5.
Theoretical probability P(A) = n(A) ÷ n(S) for equally likely outcomes. The complement: P(A′) = 1 − P(A). Probability ranges from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
Example: 4 red and 6 blue marbles. P(red) = 2/5; P(not red) = 3/5.
